name: Bilal Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What fills a normal workday for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am forty-three and lead a small crew fitting doors and doing general carpentry on building sites. My trade certificate got me started; after years of hanging doors I can hear a bad fit before I see it. I earn about the usual rate, and my partner and I have a few months of bills saved against the mortgage and our two children’s school costs. I have never used an AI tool; I would rather hold the level against the frame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a quicker order form is fine if the right hinges still turn up. An AI order cannot tell me whether a fire door drags on a building-site floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my work and pay to stay much as they are. We have one to six months of expenses saved and some other carpentry jobs nearby, which gives me room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the door crew and check each frame with a level before sign-off. I would ask the supplier for the ordinary paper delivery list because I do not use AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this picture. The daily nuisance is a late hinge box, not a machine replacing my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you look at before signing off a fire door?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check the gaps, the latch and whether the closer actually pulls it shut. A printed specification helps, but the door has to work in that opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your savings change your decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They cover a few months, not a life of idleness. For a modest ordering change, I would carry on working and leave that reserve for a real interruption.

say: I would **accept** faster ordering while keeping physical checks on each installed door.
I would **tell** my crew the frame must work in the actual opening.
think: Our **savings** and nearby jobs make this small change manageable.
I would **still** rather use a delivery list than learn AI for routine ordering.
do: **Keep** leading door installations and checking gaps, latch and closer.
**Request** ordinary supplier list for every door delivery.
feel: **Calm** because paid site work looks secure.
S0.quote: An AI order cannot tell me whether a fire door drags on a building-site floor.
fieldNote: **Bilal** trusts physical fit and has never used an AI tool.
**Typical** wages, several months of savings and some local carpentry jobs support calm in the plateau.

steps.text: Keep leading and checking building-site door installations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office will buy hinges and plan visits faster, while our crew still fits the doors. I would ask the manager whether quicker plans also mean tighter site hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can imagine a rushed delivery schedule leaving us with gaps between paid jobs. Our reserve could cover a short pause, but I do not want the builder using software to shave the crew’s rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the door work and ask for written schedules and rates before accepting new targets. I would compare the actual hours over three jobs, then speak to the manager if paid time drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about possible lost site hours, though I have a little money and some nearby work to fall back on. I am not keen to learn the office tool just to prove I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why compare three jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One late delivery can be bad luck; three jobs show whether the paid wait keeps happening. The AI office plan could be neat while my door crew waits unpaid for hinges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the schedule really cuts hours, what is next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the old rate on the new schedule. If that fails, I would apply to a posted local carpentry vacancy only if its pay covers our mortgage and school costs.

say: I would **ask** if faster planning changes our paid door-fitting hours.
I would **bring** actual hours from three jobs to the manager.
think: A **shorter** paid week is possible even though fitting remains hands-on.
A **few** months of savings buy time to check terms, not permission to accept lower rates.
do: **Track** paid door-fitting hours across three building jobs.
**Ask** manager for written schedule and wage terms while keeping shifts.
**Apply** for posted local carpentry vacancy only at household-covering pay if hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic hours loss, with reserve and local options.
S1.quote: The AI office plan could be neat while my door crew waits unpaid for hinges.
fieldNote: He **responds** through measured hours and a wage discussion rather than learning AI.
The **credible** threat is a management schedule that reduces his paid days, not immediate robot replacement.

steps.text: Keep door shifts while tracking actual paid hours
Apply for posted local carpentry role with household-covering pay if hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI in 2028, when I am forty-five, cannot swing a door into an opening. Around 2031, when I am forty-eight, capable robots could take the simple installations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry the builder might cut our paid doors before anyone knows whether a robot can manage crooked frames. A robot might hang the easy building doors in 2031; my mortgage still needs the difficult ones to pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working and ask the manager for the paid installation plan through 2031. If robot work cuts our shifts in its first year, I would trim optional spending and apply to posted nearby repair-carpentry jobs only at a wage that covers household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, because I may lose hours but can still act. I would not buy a robot course on a promise or leave a paid role first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a repair crew do that worries you less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Older door openings are often out of square and need careful fitting by hand. That might last longer, though I would want to see an actual vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What spending would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would delay a nonurgent room repaint. The school travel and mortgage stay in the budget as long as paid work allows.

say: **Thinking** AI comes in 2028; hands-on door robots are the 2031 worry.
I would **demand** a clear paid-hours plan before changing work.
think: **Routine** installations might shrink, but I still see physical repair work.
**Savings** buy months to search; a posted local job and adequate wage determine whether I move.
do: **Ask** builder for written paid door-fitting hours through 2031.
**Delay** nonurgent room repaint if robot installations cut paid shifts.
**Apply** to posted nearby repair role only at mortgage-covering pay after cuts.
feel: **Anxious** about possible hours loss, with time to search.
S2.quote: A robot might hang the easy building doors in 2031; my mortgage still needs the difficult ones to pay.
fieldNote: He **separates** 2028 thinking automation from 2031 physical installation.
**Moderate** savings and nearby jobs offer some control, but his refusal to gamble on training limits his options.

steps.text: Keep paid door shifts while seeking written future hours
Cut room repaint spending after actual shift loss
Apply for posted local repair job at household-covering wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2031 thinking AI changes ordering when I am forty-eight, and 2034 robots reach hands-on door fitting when I am fifty-one. I would rather watch a real site demonstration than sign up for every course advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn formal fire-door inspection if the builder funded it and paid the training days. A fire-door certificate is worth little if the course takes my pay and no local inspector job exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the door crew and ask whether a funded, paid-time fire-door inspection course has an actual place. If it does, I would enroll; after completing it, I would apply only to posted local inspection work paying enough for the mortgage and school bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the later robots and anxious if our hours could shrink. Five years is useful because I can demand real terms before changing course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the inspection course add to your experience?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would give me the formal checks and sign-off rules for fire doors. I know a bad gap by eye, but a certificate could let me take responsibility for the recorded inspection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course costs nothing but takes unpaid days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on paid installations. A few months saved is for an interruption, not to subsidise a builder’s staffing plan.

say: The 2031 **office** change comes before 2034 hands-on robots.
I would **consider** a formal inspection course only with funding and paid time.
think: **Experience** with door gaps is valuable, but a formal inspection role needs a credential.
I **need** a posted nearby inspection job at a wage that keeps our mortgage paid.
do: **Enroll** in funded fire-door inspection course only with paid training days.
**Keep** paid door-fitting shifts during any course.
**Apply** after completion to posted local inspection role at household-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about potential hours loss, with more time and a conditional plan.
S3.quote: A fire-door certificate is worth little if the course takes my pay and no local inspector job exists.
fieldNote: His **training** is conditional on both funding and paid time; an enquiry alone would not be retraining.
He **continues** familiar work while requiring a real nearby vacancy and adequate wage before moving.

steps.text: Enroll if actual place offered on funded fire-door course with paid days
Keep paid door shifts during course
Apply after qualification to posted local inspection job at household-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI in 2036 reaches me at fifty-three, and capable robots arrive around 2039 when I am fifty-six. I would rather hang another building door than buy a course for a robot job nobody has advertised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would prefer to stay in carpentry for as long as there is paid work. I would consider inspection later if a funded course on paid time and a posted local wage make it sensible, but I cannot assume it will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fitting and inspecting each door with the crew. I would add a new amount from each paid month to our mortgage reserve after normal bills, and take a funded paid-time inspection course only if a suitable posted local job is available to pursue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about machines at the end of the decade, but more secure about the next few years. A real paid job matters more than a distant forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you build the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would transfer a new amount from each paid month after mortgage and school costs. We would not count the money already saved as progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train if no employer posts inspection work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would keep the carpentry shifts and ask again when a real local vacancy at an adequate wage appears.

say: A **decade** lets me continue skilled door work and add to our reserve.
I would **consider** inspection only when paid training and a real local opening align.
think: I **prefer** familiar carpentry and do not need to gamble on a forecast today.
The **mortgage** reserve must grow from new wages, not from relabelling existing savings.
do: **Keep** fitting and checking site doors while paid work remains.
**Save** new money from paid months after mortgage and school bills.
**Complete** funded paid-time inspection course only for posted adequate local role.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant robots, with current work and money fairly secure.
S4.quote: I would rather hang another building door than buy a course for a robot job nobody has advertised.
fieldNote: The **longer** horizon supports actual new saving from wages and patient continuation of skilled site work.
His **resistance** to speculative training persists; even later study requires funding, paid time and a posted adequate vacancy.

steps.text: Keep fitting and checking building-site doors
Save new pay each month after household bills
Complete funded paid-time inspection course for posted adequate local role

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028/2031 picture troubles me most because routine door work could shrink while the mortgage stays. Written paid-hour plans and a posted nearby repair or inspection role paying our bills would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the manager who pays for any promised course days. If I lose site wages to take a course, a few months of savings will go quickly. A level in my hand tells me more about a building door than a course advert on my phone.

headlineQuote: A level in my hand tells me more about a building door than a course advert on my phone.
portrait: **Bilal** is a forty-three-year-old lead carpenter, trade certified and skilled in fitting building-site doors.
**Typical** pay, one to six months of savings, a mortgage and two schoolchildren shape his caution.
**Some** similar local jobs offer options, though he has never used AI and prefers familiar tools.
He **tracks** real paid hours and considers inspection only with funded paid training and a posted adequate vacancy.
biggestWorry: **Fast** hands-on robots around 2031 could reduce routine door-fitting hours before his mortgage is paid.
whatWouldHelp: **Written** paid-hour terms and a posted local repair or inspection job at household-covering wages would help.
